Kilauea. The active shield volcano on the southeastern part of the Big Island of Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. In Hawaiian religion and oral tradition, it is the sacred home of Pele, the goddess of fire and volcanoes, who is believed to reside within the Halemaʻumaʻu crater at the volcano's summit. The volcano's name translates to spewing or much spreading in the Hawaiian language, describing its frequent and fluid lava flows. From 1983 to 2018, Kilauea experienced a near-continuous 35-year eruption from the Puʻu ʻŌʻō vent, which sent vast flows of basaltic lava down the rift zone, creating new coastline and destroying several towns. In 2018, it underwent a major summit collapse which dramatically enlarged the Halemaʻumaʻu crater, drained the lava lake, and triggered destructive eruptions in the Lower East Rift Zone. The volcano hosts the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, established in 1912 by geologist Thomas Jaggar on the rim of the Kilauea caldera, making it one of the most heavily monitored volcanoes in the world. Kilauea sits on the massive neighboring shield volcano Mauna Loa, against whose flank it is built.
